case.label: B
case.text: B adds self-healing through an Auto Scaling group, which a candidate may read as 'highly available'; but every replacement launches in the same zone, so B does not survive the zone failure that the stem names. C is also the only option that does not keep a single zone, so the cue 'if one Availability Zone fails' points straight at it. No second answer holds.

case.label: C
case.text: C avoids cross-zone data transfer charges, because each zone uses its own NAT gateway, and a candidate may count that as a cost saving. But the stem says the traffic volume is small and that an interruption during a zone failure is acceptable, so the hourly charge of two extra NAT gateways outweighs the small cross-zone charge. The stem states both deciding constraints, so A is the single best answer.

case.label: D
case.text: D also gives employees temporary credentials through SAML federation with the existing identity provider, and it meets the security requirement. It fails 'centrally manage from one place' and 'LEAST operational overhead', because the roles are updated by hand in each of the 30 accounts. The words 'by hand' in D make the overhead explicit, so C stays the single answer.

case.label: A
case.text: A interface endpoint is also private and also removes the NAT gateway data processing charges. It loses only on cost, because an interface endpoint has hourly and per-GB charges while a gateway endpoint for S3 does not. The stem says the uploads come only from the instances in the VPC, which removes the one reason to prefer an interface endpoint, so B is the single answer.

case.label: C
case.text: C NAT instances in each zone with a failover script give highly available internet access without public IP addresses, so C meets the functional requirements. It fails the stated constraint that the team does not want to patch or replace network devices, because NAT instances are EC2 instances that the team must patch and replace. The stem names that constraint, so D is the single answer.

case.label: D
case.text: D is the cheapest design with no public IP addresses, and when one zone fails the instances in that zone are down anyway. But if the zone that holds the single NAT gateway fails, the instances in the other two zones lose internet access, which breaks 'Internet access must continue if one Availability Zone fails'. A adds a second NAT gateway per zone with no stated need, so C is the single answer.

case.label: E
case.text: E also removes long-term credentials and keeps least privilege, because each role holds only the read policy for the one bucket. It loses on 'LEAST operational overhead', because many identical roles and policy copies must be kept in step. B refers to 'the role', so it needs a create-role step; C is the only least-privilege role, which pairs B with C. No second pair holds.

answers.flag: The stem does not say how the data center uploads reach Amazon S3 today (a private virtual interface into the VPC, a transit gateway, or a public virtual interface); if they use a public virtual interface they already avoid the internet and the NAT gateway, and then the gateway endpoint in C is the cheaper answer for the only traffic that pays NAT charges.

case.label: C
case.text: C removes all NAT gateway data processing charges for the instance uploads, which are the only uploads that the stem says pass through the NAT gateway, and a gateway endpoint has no hourly or per-GB charge, while D adds per-GB charges on the large instance uploads. The data center servers can reach S3 over a Direct Connect public virtual interface without the internet, so 'privately' can hold without D. The intended answer depends on an unstated assumption that the on-premises uploads must enter through the VPC.

case.label: B
case.text: B a bastion host is a common pattern for reaching private instances, and the private instances themselves get no direct inbound SSH from the internet. But B opens port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 to the bastion, which is inbound SSH from the internet to the VPC, and it does not record sessions. Session Manager in private subnets also needs a path to the Systems Manager endpoints, which the stem does not state, but no other option works at all.

case.label: A
case.text: A also blocks the address range, and blocking it in every subnet is stronger defense in depth. It fails 'in the subnets of the load balancer' and 'LEAST operational overhead', because the rule is repeated for every current and new subnet. E reads well but security groups have allow rules only, so E cannot block the range. C and D remain the single pair.

case.label: D
case.text: D uses the same SCP and gives the same protection to the 40 member accounts, including their root users, and attaching per account lets the team exclude an account later. It loses only on overhead: 40 attachments now, and a new attachment for every new account, while one attachment at the root covers all member accounts. The management account is outside SCPs in both options, and the stem asks about member accounts only.

case.label: C
case.text: C is cheaper than E because it adds no second NAT gateway, and the application itself survives a zone failure through B. But if the first zone fails, the one NAT gateway fails with it and the instances in the second zone lose outbound internet access, which the stem requires to keep working. A is a Region-level design that the stem says is not required, so B and E are the single pair.
